lessons: Hook lines that pose a surprising question or vivid image (e.g., "This shark is older than the United States", "Why Scientists Missed an Outer Kuiper Belt") correspond to the highest 10% retention (>1.5).
Hooks that include a concrete sensory cue or unexpected comparison (e.g., "Gulping ice water after a hot pepper feels like relief") keep viewers above the average 10% retention (~1.2).
Lines that immediately launch into a detailed explanation or repeat the title tend to appear in the biggest drop points (e.g., dead‑skin swelling, node definition).
Videos that avoid a visible countdown timer generally have higher retention; the few videos with a countdown show mixed or lower end‑retention values.
Drop points frequently occur around 10‑15% of the video when the script shifts from the hook to a slower, fact‑heavy segment; keeping the narrative fast‑paced here improves hold.
worst_moment_types: Straight‑forward scientific explanation without a hook (e.g., definition of nodes, dead‑skin swelling).
Repeated phrasing of the title or question that adds no new information.
Long pause or “guess” prompts that stall the narrative.
best_hook_types: Unexpected, sensory‑rich statements that create a visual or feeling contrast.
Provocative questions that promise a surprising answer.
Brief, punchy fact that challenges common knowledge.
